specifically, I've always wanted to fly a Cessna 172R, but seems out of reach for the moment.
Any pilots out there want to share their experience with Cessna?

I'm a commercial pilot with like 4,000 hours. The first 650 hours were mostly in Cessnas ranging from 150s to 210s. I only have like an hour with a G1000.

172s are great! They've been around for over 50 years and are still made to this day - in fact, they're the most manufactured aircraft of all time. It's safe to say we've worked out all the important bugs.

Everybody's flown one. They're so popular, almost any pilot will have flown one at least a little, so there is a huge wealth of experience.

Parts are everywhere. They're so popular, maintenance is easily available, because mechanics have as much experience with them as pilots. If you want an aftermarket modification, there are probably a half dozen people who make it.

It works. It holds four people so you can take the family, it holds cargo, it can go for hours,doesn't burn a ton of fuel, takes off and lands in a relatively short distance... It just has a great overall package.

Having said that...

The problem Cessna faces is they are having to compete with Cessna. The aircraft are so good, you can't make a new Cessna and sell it for as cheaply as you can get a lovely 1977 Cessna, so they have to differentiate themselves.

Unfortunately, they chose the G1000. Like I said, I only have like an hour with it, but it sucks donkey balls. Everything was complicated,mhard to find, hard to understand, and totally unnecessary. My feeling is they're trying to make people these days feel like airline pilots with a bunch of whiz-bang technology, and by doing this they neglect teaching people how to fly the damn airplane. When you're learning you need to look outside at the world, see and avoid, use ded reckoning, and learn how to feel the airplane. The G1000 added 5 hours onto primary flight training at our school just from being so complicated.

The other problem is the G1000 is a stupid computer. If something breaks, often times it'll disable half the systems with red Xs, and your flight is cancelled. On a normal aircraft with "steam gauges" you mark it as inop and can probably continue. When maintenance fixes it, they pop the gauge out and pop a new one in (fancy modular technology!) On the G1000, you call an avionics shop (which is different from a regular mechanic, and less likely to be on the field) and schedule a visit from them.

So to sum up: C172s are great, G1000s suck donkeyballs.
